result: The authors successfully reconstituted microtubule minus end-directed mRNA transport in vitro using only four purified components: Egl, BicD, dynein, and dynactin. This minimal system achieved 80% processive transport of hairy RNA and also supported transport of I-factor RNA, demonstrating that no additional proteins are required for this process.
evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C44, C47-C48, C54, and C102 collectively demonstrate successful reconstitution with purified components. The quantitative data (80% processive transport, Figure 1C-D) and component omission experiments (Figure 2B-C) provide strong evidence. The co-transport of all labeled components (C54) and lack of requirement for additional factors (C48, C102) are well-documented.

result: The reconstituted transport system retains selectivity for RNA localization signals, with the ILS binding to microtubules ~5-fold more frequently than scrambled RNA and exhibiting similar increases in processive movements. However, ~75% of scrambled RNA transport events co-localized with ILS, suggesting indirect transport through association with active ILS-bound complexes.
evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by quantitative data in Figure 1E-H showing differential binding and transport of ILS vs scrambled RNA. The co-localization analysis (C52) provides mechanistic insight into the modest transport of scrambled RNA. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.0001).

result: All three protein complexes (Egl/BICD2, dynactin, and dynein) are simultaneously required to link RNA to microtubules. Omission of any component nearly abolished RNA-microtubule association, though dynein could still bind microtubules weakly without Egl/BICD2 or dynactin. The combination of Egl/BICD2 and dynactin increased dynein microtubule binding ~2-fold.
evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are well-supported by systematic component omission experiments shown in Figure 2B-D. The quantitative measurements of binding events and statistical analysis (ANOVA with Dunnett's correction, p<0.0001) provide rigorous evidence for the requirement of all components.

result: RNA is required for robust activation of dynein motility in the presence of Egl/BicD and dynactin. The presence of RNA increased processive dynein movements ~6-fold, enhanced microtubule binding, increased the propensity for processive movement, and significantly increased mean velocity and run length. This effect was observed with both mammalian BICD2 and Drosophila BicD, indicating evolutionary conservation.
evaluation: Claims C6, C60-C71, and C104 are strongly supported by comprehensive quantitative data in Figure 3. The ~6-fold increase in processive movements (Figure 3A-B), enhanced binding (Figure 3C), increased processivity (Figure 3D), and improved velocity/run length (Figure 3E-F) are all statistically significant (p<0.0001). The effect is reproduced with Egl/DmBicD (Figure 3G-J), demonstrating robustness.

result: RNA promotes assembly of the Egl/BICD2/dynein/dynactin complex. The frequency of Egl co-localization with microtubule-bound dynein increased ~6-fold in the presence of RNA, and similar effects were observed for BICD2. Immunoprecipitation from Drosophila embryo extracts confirmed that RNA addition led to detectable co-precipitation of dynein and dynactin with Egl::GFP.
evaluation: Claims C72-C77 and C106 are supported by both in vitro single-molecule imaging (Figure 4A-C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and biochemical experiments (Figure 4D-E). The ~6-fold increase in co-localization is quantified with appropriate statistics (Welch's t-test, p<0.0001). The immunoprecipitation provides orthogonal validation in a native context.

result: The interaction of Egl with the LC8 dynein light chain is not required for RNA-directed activation of dynein motility. A mutant Egl/BICD2 complex (Egldlc2pt) lacking LC8-binding capability still supported robust hairy RNA transport and RNA-induced increases in processive movement, microtubule binding, velocity, and run length.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 and C105 are well-supported by experiments with the Egldlc2pt mutant shown in Figure 5. The mutant complex exhibits similar RNA-dependent activation as wild-type (compare Figure 5C-E to Figure 3), with statistical significance maintained (p<0.0001). This definitively rules out a role for the Egl-LC8 interaction in this process.

result: The RNA localization signal promotes and stabilizes the interaction of Egl with BicD. The ILS caused large increases in mean molar mass of Egl/BICD2 complexes as measured by SE-AUC and SEC-MALS, while scrambled RNA had minimal effect. This was associated with enhanced interaction of BICD2 and Egl, and similar effects were observed with Egl/DmBicD, indicating that the complexes readily equilibrate with constituent species in the absence of RNA.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C82-C89 are supported by multiple biophysical techniques (SE-AUC in Figure 6A, SEC-MALS in Figure 6B-D). The large increases in molar mass with ILS vs scrambled RNA demonstrate selectivity (C85-C86). SDS-PAGE analysis confirms enhanced Egl-BicD interaction (C87, Figure 6B). The use of orthogonal methods strengthens the conclusions.

result: Active transport complexes contain a single BicD dimer associated with two Egl molecules. Dual-labeling experiments showed 39% of motile BICD2 complexes and 37% of motile Egl complexes were dual-labeled, consistent with one BICD2 dimer and two Egl molecules per complex after correction for labeling efficiency. Even in the absence of RNA, motile complexes contained two Egl molecules, suggesting that occupancy of both Egl-binding sites on BicD CC3 favors relief of autoinhibition.
evaluation: Claims C9, C90-C95, C99, C101, and C117 are supported by sophisticated dual-labeling stoichiometry experiments (Figure 7B-E). The observed percentages (39% for BICD2, 37% for Egl) match theoretical predictions for the proposed stoichiometry after correction for labeling efficiency (Supplementary files 1-2). The consistency across different labeling schemes and with/without RNA strengthens the conclusions.

result: Most active transport complexes associate with a single RNA molecule. Dual-labeling experiments with Cy3-hairy and Cy5-hairy RNA showed 14% of motile RNPs had signals from both dyes, which after correction for labeling efficiency indicates 30% of RNPs contained two RNAs and 70% contained one RNA.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97 and C100 are supported by dual-labeling experiments in Figure 7F-G. The calculations accounting for labeling efficiency and the possibility of two dyes of the same color are detailed in Supplementary file 3. The result is consistent with previous findings in extracts (C98), though the in vitro system shows some non-specific RNA association.

result: A purified Egl/BicD complex does not efficiently associate with dynein and dynactin in the absence of RNA, and RNA-bound Egl must overcome BicD autoinhibition. The most parsimonious explanation is that the RNA localization signal promotes occupancy of CC3 with Egl, thereby freeing CC1/2 to interact with dynein and dynactin.
evaluation: Claims C103, C107, and C116 represent the central mechanistic model supported by the collective data. The poor association without RNA (C103) is demonstrated in Figures 3-4, the requirement for RNA to overcome autoinhibition (C107) is shown throughout, and the proposed mechanism (C116) is consistent with all observations including stoichiometry (two Egl per BicD dimer), biophysical data (RNA stabilizes Egl-BicD interaction), and functional data (RNA-dependent activation).

result: The RNA-mediated activation mechanism is consistent with previous structural and functional studies. The recruitment of RNA to dynein by Egl/BICD2 is dependent on dynactin, and RNA-bound Egl/BICD2 augments dynein's microtubule binding, velocity, and run length similarly to BICD2N. Recent studies suggest that a single BICD2N dimer can recruit one or two dynein complexes, with two motors present in the majority of transport RNPs.
evaluation: Claims C108-C112 integrate the current findings with previous literature. The dependence on dynactin (C109, Figure 2B-C) and similarity to BICD2N effects (C110, Figure 3) are demonstrated. The citations to contemporary studies (C108, C111-C112) provide appropriate context, though these claims rely heavily on prior work rather than new data from this study.

result: The mechanism of RNA-mediated activation of dynein through relief of adaptor autoinhibition is distinct from mechanisms proposed for other systems, such as the yeast actin-based mRNA transport complex where RNA-dependent dimerization of myosin monomers was proposed. Multiple strategies may have evolved to coordinate motor processivity with RNA cargo availability.
evaluation: Claims C113-C115 appropriately contextualize the findings within the broader field. The comparison to the yeast system (C113-C114) is supported by citations, and the speculation about multiple evolved strategies (C115) is reasonable given the evidence. However, these are primarily comparative/speculative claims rather than new experimental findings.

result: Free Egl is monomeric as determined by SEC-MALS analysis.
evaluation: Claim C118 is supported by SEC-MALS data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3, showing an observed molar mass of 112.0 ± 1.7 kDa matching the predicted molar mass of 112 kDa for monomeric Egl. This is a straightforward biophysical measurement.

result: BicD proteins are implicated in transport of diverse cellular cargoes and pathogens by dynein and dynactin, and BicD CC3 can simultaneously bind two Rab6GTP proteins, suggesting that cargo-mediated scaffolding of adaptor assemblies may be a general mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are supported by appropriate citations to previous work. These claims provide context for the broader significance of the findings but do not present new experimental data from this study. The speculation about general mechanisms is reasonable but not directly tested here.

result: Polarized mRNA transport is a prevalent mechanism for spatial control of protein synthesis that contributes to diverse processes including embryonic axis determination, epithelial polarity, and neuronal plasticity. However, the composition of transported RNPs and regulation of their movement, particularly the mechanisms of mRNA recruitment to microtubule motors, remain poorly understood.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C11-C14 establish the biological context and knowledge gaps that motivate the study. These are well-established facts in the field supported by appropriate citations and represent accurate characterizations of the state of knowledge.

result: In Drosophila, mRNA transport depends on Egl, BicD, dynein, and dynactin. Egl is a 1004-amino-acid protein that directly associates with RNA localization signals through an exonuclease-like domain (residues 557-726), uses its N-terminal region to bind BicD, and uses C-terminal features to bind LC8. Mammalian BicD orthologues associate with dynein and dynactin, but it is not known if other factors cooperate with Egl and BicD to bridge mRNAs to the motor complex.
evaluation: Claims C15-C24 accurately summarize previous knowledge about the Drosophila mRNA transport system with appropriate citations. These establish the foundation for the current study's investigations and correctly identify the knowledge gap (C24) that the study addresses.

result: The isolated N-terminal region of mammalian BICD2 (BICD2N) forms an extended coiled-coil homodimer that bridges dynein and dynactin, dramatically increasing processive movement, velocity, and force output. This mechanism is evolutionarily conserved, as the equivalent region of Drosophila BicD stimulates dynein-based transport in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C25-C32 accurately summarize well-established findings from previous studies with appropriate citations. These provide essential background for understanding BicD function and the significance of the current study's findings about full-length BicD regulation.

result: Full-length BicD proteins interact poorly with dynein and dynactin and are weak activators of dynein motility, apparently due to autoinhibition by CC3 folding back onto CC1/2. Previous models proposed that cargo-binding proteins like Egl or Rab6GTP binding to CC3 relieve this autoinhibition. While Rab6 only binds BicD when GTP-bound (induced by membrane association), Egl can associate with BicD CC3 in vitro without RNA, suggesting RNA might not be involved in relieving autoinhibition.
evaluation: Claims C33-C43 accurately summarize previous models and observations with appropriate citations. The inference in C43 that RNA is not involved represents the prevailing hypothesis that the current study challenges, making this an important setup for the study's key findings.

result: Hairy RNAs accumulated at microtubule minus ends following transport and were capable of diffusive motion on the microtubule lattice, consistent with previous observations in Drosophila extract-based systems.
evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-B and are consistent with previous findings (citation to Soundararajan and Bullock, 2014). These observations validate that the reconstituted system recapitulates key features of the native system.

result: Transported hairy RNPs assembled in Drosophila extracts exclusively contain a single RNA, as previously reported.
evaluation: Claim C98 is supported by citations to previous studies by the same group. This provides important context for interpreting the finding that 30% of in vitro reconstituted RNPs contain two RNAs, suggesting some non-specific RNA association in the purified system.

result: Scaffolding of adaptor protein assemblies by cargoes is an attractive mechanism for regulating intracellular transport.
evaluation: Claim C10 is explicitly speculative ("attractive mechanism") and represents a proposed general principle extrapolated from the specific findings. While the data support this model for the Egl/BicD/RNA system, the generality to other transport systems is not directly tested and remains a hypothesis for future investigation.

result: The Drosophila Egl/Rab6GTP-binding site in BicD has 71% identity and 93% similarity with mouse and human sequences. Co-expression of BICD2 greatly increased the amount of soluble Egl, with extremely low yield when Egl was expressed alone. The purified Egl/BICD2 complex contained little if any co-purified RNA based on A260:A280 ratios.
evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplements 1-2. These are straightforward technical observations that validate the experimental system: the sequence conservation justifies using mammalian BICD2 with Drosophila Egl (C121), the co-expression requirement demonstrates protein interdependence (C122-C123), and the lack of co-purified RNA ensures a clean starting point for RNA addition experiments (C124).
